ModelCharacter: The smallest current Duffy hull: a Spencer Lincoln-influenced Maine Downeast boat built around a single inboard diesel, full keel and genuine commercial-lobsterboat heritage. Individual boats range from sparse workboats and launches to carefully finished pocket cruisers, so the hull identity is far more standardized than the accommodations.
DesignLineage: The Duffy 26 entered the Atlantic Boat/Duffy line in 1986.
Atlantic Boat states that more than 50 Duffy 26 hulls have served as lobsterboats, tow boats, charter boats, launches and pleasure boats.
The same hull is currently offered by Atlantic Boat as a Duffy kit and is also used for commercial launch configurations.
Because Duffy hulls may be completed by Atlantic Boat, other finish yards or owners, B-Atlas treats 'Duffy 26' as a hull-family identity rather than assuming one factory interior.
OwnershipCharacter: Single-diesel shaft propulsion and a commercial-derived hull make ownership mechanically simple. The main variability comes from who finished the boat: wiring, tanks, cabinetry, deckhouse construction and cruising systems can differ dramatically between two Duffy 26s.

ModelCharacter: The direct continuation of the Prairie 36 Coastal Cruiser after Atlantic Yachts acquired Prairie's molds and tooling in 1982. It is a traditional Hargrave-designed soft-chine semi-displacement double-cabin trawler with full-length keel, two private staterooms and unusually good machinery access.
DesignLineage: Prairie built the 36 Coastal Cruiser from 1979 until closing in early 1982.
Atlantic Yachts acquired the Prairie 36 molds/tooling and reintroduced the same design as the Atlantic 37 Double Cabin in 1982.
The Atlantic 37 continued through 1992 with several single/twin diesel engine options.
This is direct Prairie 36 → Atlantic 37 lineage, not merely stylistic resemblance.
OwnershipCharacter: A straightforward classic trawler platform with strong hull lineage, protected running gear and roomy engine access. Twin-engine examples cost more to service than the Prairie's smaller-power versions, while teak, tanks, windows and 1980s systems dominate refit risk.

ModelCharacter: A substantial 1970s Cheoy Lee flybridge trawler with broad beam, heavy fiberglass construction, twin or single diesel examples and traditional teak decks/interior. It sits between the compact sedan trawlers and Cheoy Lee's larger long-range motor-yacht families.
DesignLineage: Surviving 1974–81 boats are consistently documented as Cheoy Lee 36 Trawlers, with some European records using 'Traveller 36'.
Period records show both single- and twin-diesel installations, indicating propulsion varied across boats or sub-generations.
The 36 is broader and substantially heavier than the 32/35 family and should be treated as a distinct hull/model identity.
Factory model-generation labels such as 'Mk II' are not sufficiently documented to use as B-Atlas's canonical name, so the record is normalized to Cheoy Lee 36 Trawler.
OwnershipCharacter: A sturdy, comfortable cruiser with strong low-speed manners, but twin-engine examples, extensive teak and very large tankage create materially higher ownership demands than the 32/35. Exact machinery and layout should be verified hull by hull.

ModelVariations.Description: Factory-era material uses Open Fisherman and later Open Sportsman terminology for the open cockpit member of the 28 family. B-Atlas retains Open Fisherman as the canonical historic name and keeps Open Sportsman as a search alias.

ModelCharacter: The cockpit-first member of the Cape Dory 28 family: an open Down East fisherman with the same protected semi-displacement hull as the cruisers, but substantially less enclosed superstructure and a large working cockpit.
DesignLineage: The Open Fisherman shares the Cape Dory 28 hull with the Flybridge Cruiser, Power Cruiser and 280 Sport.
Factory and later Newport literature also use Open Sportsman terminology for this open-cockpit configuration.
The Open retains V-berths, a compact galley and enclosed head despite its fishing-oriented deck arrangement.
It is a genuine factory configuration rather than a stripped Flybridge Cruiser.
OwnershipCharacter: Simpler topside and easier to use for fishing, swimming or day cruising than the enclosed 28s. The same hull/deck-core and vintage-system issues apply, but there is less cabin/flybridge structure to maintain.

ModelCharacter: The smaller sister to the Cape Dory 36 PowerYacht: a handsome Clive Dent-designed twin-diesel flybridge cruiser with full-length keel, wide side decks, lower helm and a single private forward stateroom.
DesignLineage: Cape Dory introduced the 33 PowerYacht in 1988 as a smaller companion to the established 36.
Factory history records 22 Cape Dory-built examples; Powerboat Guide tracks the broader 1988–1994 production lineage through the Newport Shipyards transition.
The 33 uses the same New England-style modified-V, protective-keel design philosophy as the 30 and 36 PowerYachts.
Robinhood Marine later produced the design under license as the Robinhood 33.
OwnershipCharacter: A practical couple's cruiser with safe deck circulation and useful 16–20-knot performance. Twin diesels, two helm stations and aging teak/electrical systems create more maintenance than the single-engine 28 family.

ModelCharacter: A distinctive flush-deck, full-displacement DeFever designed for genuine offshore range: two private staterooms separated by a near-standing engine room, enormous tankage, single-level side/aft decks and twin Lehman diesels cruising at seven to eight knots.
DesignLineage: The 43 Trawler was produced from 1978–1981 and is one of DeFever's unusual flush-deck designs.
Its aft deck and side decks are on one level rather than using the raised aft-cabin/sundeck arrangement common to many Taiwan trawlers.
The galley-aft salon arrangement reflects Arthur DeFever's preference for keeping food preparation close to outdoor living spaces.
The model is a distinct full-displacement offshore cruiser and not a renamed 41.
OwnershipCharacter: Extremely capable for slow long-range cruising, with more than 1,000 gallons of fuel and 500 gallons of water, but that capability comes with 40,000-plus pounds of boat and extensive teak. Tank integrity, deck condition, twin-engine systems and haul-out infrastructure are major ownership considerations.

ModelCharacter: The current R-25 is a new-generation outboard cruiser, not a continuation of the old diesel R-25 mechanically. It combines an 8'6" trailerable beam, a 250-hp Yamaha and a clear-path swim platform with full cruising amenities.
DesignLineage: Ranger revived the R-25 name for a modern outboard design after the diesel Classic/SC generations.
The current boat uses a planing outboard hull and clear-path swim-platform architecture.
It sits between the R-23 and R-27 in today's Ranger lineup.
Shared model number should not be interpreted as shared hull or drivetrain with the diesel R-25s.
OwnershipCharacter: Outboard serviceability and true highway-width trailering simplify ownership, while higher cruising speed increases fuel use and the outboard occupies the transom area.

Strengths: Well-regarded Northwest fiberglass construction
Practical cockpit, lower helm and flybridge arrangement
Good interior utility without heavy trawler-style exterior teak
Weaknesses: Substantial overall weight requires serious horsepower tracking, engine fuel consumption spikes on active plane.
CommonProblems: Exhaust riser pipe internal scaling, rudder post stuffing box packing line leakage.
TypicalMission: Extended bluewater coastal passage making, long-term cruising, and remote family loops.
AvoidIf: You require a full-displacement trawler
You insist on single-diesel simplicity
You are unwilling to verify original versus repowered machinery
Overview: The Tollycraft 37 Sedan is a Pacific Northwest-built fiberglass flybridge sedan emphasizing practical cockpit use, broad visibility and solid cruising construction. Unlike traditional displacement trawlers, these boats use modified-V powerboat hulls and were offered with gasoline and, on some configurations, diesel power.

CoupleCruising.Summary: The documented cruising layout is practical for a couple; guest capacity and privacy vary by model.

SoloHandling.Summary: Lower-helm access and protected decks can help short-handed operation, but windage, engine count and docking equipment remain hull-specific.

InlandWaterways.Summary: Route fit depends on actual beam, draft and air draft; verify bridge and marina limits for the individual boat.

ExposedWater.Summary: Condition, loading and actual hull configuration are decisive; this assessment reflects documented design intent rather than an offshore guarantee.

ModelVariations.Name: Engine and bridge arrangements
ModelVariations.Description: Tollycraft models commonly appeared with different gasoline/diesel packages and bridge layouts; individual equipment must be verified.

ModelCharacter: A heavy, broad-beam Pacific Northwest sedan cruiser from Tollycraft's 1970s era, combining a modified-V hull, twin direct-drive engines, large salon windows and practical flybridge/cockpit circulation in a boat renowned for rough-water confidence.
DesignLineage: Surviving market records and the Canadian Tollycruisers fleet archive establish the 37 Sedan as a distinct Tollycraft model, with about 150 built.
Verified examples span 1974–1980.
The 37 belongs to Tollycraft's older sedan/convertible generation and is not the same model as the later 34 Sport Sedan.
Gasoline and diesel propulsion are both common in the surviving fleet, with many boats repowered during their long service lives.
OwnershipCharacter: A rugged, straightforward cruiser with excellent owner-community support and conventional shaft machinery. Nearly every surviving boat has decades of upgrades, so repower quality, fuel tanks, wiring, windows and deck hardware matter more than factory engine specification.
